paras: The lynching of Massey Hill took place on the night of Saturday, November 5, 1881, when a mob took Hill, a Black man, from the jail at Manchester, Tennessee, and killed him. Hill had been accused of attempting to rape a little girl near the town, and two papers reported that he was hanged. A one-sentence Nashville dispatch carried the news across the country, where it was often printed beside the lynching of Robert Williams in South Carolina the same week.

According to the Nashville wire, Hill, described as 'colored', was held in jail for an attempted rape of 'a little girl' near Manchester. The Southern Standard of McMinnville, in its column of Coffee County news, gave a different charge: 'rape upon a white girl near Viola'. No paper named the girl, gave her age, or described any hearing or trial for Hill.

On Saturday night a mob took Hill from the jail at Manchester and lynched him. The Eaton Democrat and the Southern Standard said he was hanged, though no report named the place where he died. The Democratic Press of Ravenna, Ohio, alone described the lynchers as 'a masked mob', and no paper gave their number or names.
The coverage contains no report of an inquest, arrests or any official response.

The Memphis Daily Appeal printed the Nashville dispatch on November 6 under the headline 'Another Black Ruffian Disposed of', directly above the Williams item headed 'They Let Him Off Easy'. The Chicago Daily Tribune ran the same dispatch as 'Still Another of the Same Kind Hung Up' after its long account of the Williams lynching, and the Savannah Morning News called Hill 'A Negro Fiend'. Under later Nashville datelines the identical text appeared in the Dallas Daily Herald as 'Rapist Lynched' and in the Anderson Intelligencer as 'A Negro Lynched in Tennessee'.

Northern papers mostly ran the item as a bare news brief, and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer grouped Hill with Williams under 'Ravishers Lynched'. The Iowa Plain Dealer did not name Hill, saying only that 'similar justice' to the Greenwood lynching had been 'meted out to a colored citizen near Manchester'. The Ravenna Democratic Press, calling Hill 'a colored rapist', told readers to expect 'a howl from the Republican papers about Southern Ku Klux and bulldozers'.

Tennessee weeklies reported the lynching a week later, the Milan Exchange in its state news column and the Southern Standard among its Coffee County items. The Clarksville Weekly Chronicle called Hill 'a negro rapist' and remarked that 'Judge Lynch' had been busy that fall 'dealing out summary justice to these fiends'.

The papers differed on the charge: the wire said Hill had attempted rape, while the Southern Standard's Coffee County column said he had committed rape upon a white girl near Viola. Smaller errors also circulated, including the name 'Massey Bill' in the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Ravenna paper's placing of the lynching 'near Nashville'.

bases: A Black man accused of a sexual assault on a girl was taken from the jail at Manchester by a mob and lynched (hanged) (A2, A14, A20).
Every report says a mob took Hill from jail and lynched or hanged him (A2, A3, A20), in punishment for an alleged rape or attempted rape of a girl (A2, A20); no lawful authority is mentioned.
The Nashville wire (A2, A3) and the separate county-news column of the McMinnville Southern Standard (A20) agree that a mob took Hill from the Manchester jail and killed him.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal headed the wire 'Another Black Ruffian Disposed of' and the Savannah Morning News 'A Negro Fiend Lynched'.
The Clarksville Weekly Chronicle said 'Judge Lynch' had been busy 'dealing out summary justice to these fiends'.
The Iowa Plain Dealer called it 'similar justice' to the Greenwood, S.C., lynching of Robert Williams.
The Ravenna Democratic Press called Hill 'a colored rapist' and told readers to look out for 'a howl from the Republican papers about Southern Ku Klux and bulldozers'.
Most other papers ran the one-sentence wire item as a news brief, often next to the Williams lynching.

versions.value: attempted rape / attempted outrage on a little girl
rape upon a white girl near Viola

conflicts.note: The wire says attempt; the Southern Standard's Coffee County column says rape and is the only source to give the girl's race or the place, Viola.

versions.value: night of November 5 ('to-night' in Nov. 5 dispatches; 'Saturday night'; 'on the 5th')
'last night' under a Nashville November 7 dateline (would imply November 6)

conflicts.note: The Nov. 6 and Nov. 7 datelines repeat the same wire text with 'last night'; the Nov. 5 dispatches and the Tennessee papers agree on Saturday, November 5, so the Dallas dateline looks like a reprinting artifact.
Only the Ohio Democratic Press says 'near Nashville', apparently mistaking the dateline for the place.
'Bill' in the St. Paul Globe looks like a misreading of 'Hill'.
